# 2009 NFC Wild Card playoff game (Green Bay–Arizona)

The 2009 NFC Wild Card playoff game between the Green Bay Packers and the Arizona Cardinals was played on January 10, 2010, at University of Phoenix Stadium in Glendale, Arizona. Arizona won 51–45 in overtime, ending the game on a strip-sack and fumble return by linebacker Karlos Dansby after cornerback Michael Adams blitzed Aaron Rodgers, a sequence widely discussed in postgame coverage. The game set then-NFL playoff records for combined points (96) and combined touchdowns (13) and featured prolific quarterback performances by Kurt Warner (29-of-33, five touchdowns, no interceptions) and Aaron Rodgers (423 passing yards, four touchdowns) . Attendance was 61,926, and the referee was Scott Green . The broadcast aired on FOX and delivered 34.4 million viewers, peaking at 44.1 million .

## Background

The matchup was part of the NFL’s Wild Card round in the 2009 season. Green Bay entered as the No. 5 seed at 11–5 and Arizona as the NFC West champion at 10–6 . The teams had played in Week 17 at the same venue, with Green Bay winning 33–7; that game served as contextual prelude for the rematch one week later . Green Bay had been among the league’s most turnover-averse teams during the regular season (fewest turnovers, 16), a trend that contrasted with the early sequence of the playoff game, when the Packers committed two turnovers in the first five minutes and fell behind 14–0 .

Arizona played without three-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Anquan Boldin due to knee and ankle injuries, which shifted targets to Larry Fitzgerald, Early Doucet, and Steve Breaston . Local and national outlets later highlighted the contest as a high-scoring “shootout” and a notable entry in Arizona–Wisconsin sports history .

## Teams

- Green Bay Packers: Finished 11–5 and second in the NFC North, earning a Wild Card berth. The team won seven of its final eight regular-season games, including the 33–7 Week 17 win at Arizona . Aaron Rodgers was making his first playoff start .

- Arizona Cardinals: Won the NFC West at 10–6 and hosted the Wild Card game. Despite Boldin’s absence, Arizona’s offense featured Warner at quarterback and wide receivers Fitzgerald, Doucet, and Breaston. Rookie running back Beanie Wells contributed 92 rushing yards in the playoff game .

## Venue

The game was played at University of Phoenix Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, a venue with a retractable roof and a natural-grass playing surface that is grown on a movable field tray . Reported attendance was 61,926 .

Kickoff was promoted locally at 2:30 p.m. Arizona time; Green Bay’s pregame notes listed 3:40 p.m. CST (2:40 p.m. Arizona) .

## Broadcast

FOX televised the game. The network’s primary booth of Joe Buck and Troy Aikman is listed for the telecast . The Cardinals announced a halftime performance by the band 3 Doors Down .

The telecast drew a 19.6 household rating/34 share and 34.4 million viewers, peaking at a 24.3/37 rating and 44.1 million viewers. It ranked as the highest-rated NFL Wild Card game since 2000 and the most-viewed since 1999; in adults 18–49, the game drew a 12.2/36 . Overnight ratings reached 21.8 nationally, with local overnights of 49.1/70 in Milwaukee and 38.0/62 in Phoenix; ratings peaked at 27.0/40 from 7:45–8:00 p.m. ET .

## Game summary

Arizona opened quickly. On Green Bay’s first play, Karlos Dansby disrupted a pass that resulted in an interception by Dominique Rodgers-Cromartie, and on the next Packers possession, Adams stripped Donald Driver with Alan Branch recovering; Tim Hightower’s 1-yard run and Early Doucet’s 15-yard scoring reception established a 14–0 lead within five minutes . Neil Rackers added a 23-yard field goal late in the first quarter .

Green Bay narrowed the deficit on Rodgers’ 1-yard touchdown run, but Doucet’s second 15-yard touchdown catch extended Arizona’s lead. Mason Crosby’s 20-yard field goal as time expired made the halftime score 24–10 Cardinals .

The third quarter featured rapid scoring. Larry Fitzgerald’s 33-yard touchdown reception pushed the lead to 31–10; Green Bay responded with touchdown passes to Greg Jennings (6 yards) and Jordy Nelson (11 yards). Fitzgerald’s 11-yard touchdown restored a 38–24 margin entering the fourth quarter .

Green Bay tied the game with a 30-yard touchdown pass to James Jones and a 1-yard touchdown run by John Kuhn at 10:57 of the fourth. Warner’s 17-yard touchdown strike to Steve Breaston put Arizona ahead 45–38, and Rodgers tied the game with an 11-yard pass to Spencer Havner at 1:52. In the final seconds of regulation, Rackers missed a 34-yard field goal wide left with 0:14 remaining, sending the game to overtime .

Green Bay won the overtime coin toss and nearly ended the game on the first play when Rodgers narrowly overthrew a wide-open Jennings deep . On third-and-6 from the Packers’ 24, Adams blitzed and strip-sacked Rodgers; as the ball popped free, it deflected off Rodgers’ foot into the air, where Dansby caught it and returned it 17 yards for the walk-off touchdown at 13:42 of overtime .

Final score: Arizona Cardinals 51, Green Bay Packers 45 (OT) .

## Statistics

Team totals
- Yards: ARI 531 (156 rush, 375 net pass); GB 493 (89 rush, 404 net pass) 
- First downs: GB 32; ARI 30 
- Yards per play: ARI 9.3 (57 plays); GB 7.4 (67 plays) 
- Third down efficiency: GB 5/11; ARI 3/5 
- Fourth down efficiency: GB 2/2; ARI 0/0 
- Turnovers: GB 3 (2 fumbles lost, 1 INT); ARI 1 (1 fumble lost) 
- Sacks allowed: GB 5 for −19; ARI 1 for −4 
- Time of possession: ARI 31:27; GB 29:51 
- Punts: One by each team 

Leading individual performances
- Quarterbacks: Arizona — Kurt Warner: 29-of-33, 379 yards, 5 TD, 0 INT (154.1 rating) . Green Bay — Aaron Rodgers: 28-of-42, 423 yards, 4 TD, 1 INT, 5 sacks; plus 3 rushes, 13 yards, 1 rushing TD .
- Receivers: Arizona — Steve Breaston 7 receptions, 125 yards, 1 TD; Larry Fitzgerald 6 receptions, 82 yards, 2 TD; Early Doucet 6 receptions, 77 yards, 2 TD . Green Bay — Jermichael Finley 6 receptions, 159 yards; Greg Jennings 8 receptions, 130 yards, 1 TD; James Jones 3 receptions, 50 yards, 1 TD; Spencer Havner 2 receptions, 16 yards, 1 TD; Jordy Nelson 1 reception, 11 yards, 1 TD .
- Rushers: Arizona — Beanie Wells 14 carries, 91 yards (long 42); Tim Hightower 7 carries, 19 yards, 1 TD . Green Bay — Ryan Grant 11 carries, 64 yards; John Kuhn 1 carry, 1 yard, 1 TD; Aaron Rodgers 3 carries, 13 yards, 1 TD .
- Defense: Arizona recorded five sacks (Bertrand Berry 2.0; Chike Okeafor 1.0; Darnell Dockett 1.0; Michael Adams 1.0) and one interception (Dominique Rodgers-Cromartie) . Green Bay’s Clay Matthews had one sack .

## Records and milestones

- Combined points and touchdowns: The game set then-NFL playoff records for combined points (96) and combined touchdowns (13) .
- Franchise passing mark: Rodgers’ passing total established a Packers franchise playoff record for single-game yardage, as noted by ESPN’s NFL Nation coverage .
- Combined yardage and punts: The teams combined for 1,024 total yards and punted once each .

Subsequent sources have continued to refer to the contest as among the highest-scoring in postseason history and a prominent offensive display for both teams .

## Officiating and controversies

Scott Green served as the game’s referee, as listed by ESPN game information . The overtime sequence generated debate. On the deciding play, cornerback Michael Adams blitzed and strip-sacked Rodgers; the ball deflected off Rodgers’ foot and was returned by Dansby for the winning touchdown. Television replays suggested potential contact to the quarterback’s facemask, but no penalty was called on the field . Fan commentary and team-focused outlets criticized several aspects of officiating, including the overtime hit, while acknowledging Arizona’s effective pass rush; those views represent postgame opinion rather than official determinations . Mainstream reporting emphasized the play’s mechanics and the absence of a flag rather than presenting an official ruling beyond the game result .

## Aftermath and legacy

Arizona advanced to the NFC Divisional Round and played at top-seeded New Orleans; several outlets described the Wild Card victory as a high-scoring shootout and highlighted Warner’s postseason performance, with comments from head coach Ken Whisenhunt and Green Bay’s Mike McCarthy emphasizing the game’s competitive nature . The Week 17 rematch context was revisited in later coverage, noting the reversal of fortunes from Green Bay’s 33–7 win to the playoff outcome .

Cardinals-Packers Playoff Sunday
================================

Kickoff will be 2:30 p.m. Arizona time; Tickets on sale Monday
--------------------------------------------------------------

 Jan 03, 2010 at 01:35 PM

*   [](https://www.azcardinals.com/news/cardinals-packers-playoff-sunday-1007135 "Share on Facebook")
*   [](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Cardinals-Packers+Playoff+Sunday&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.azcardinals.com%2Fnews%2Fcardinals-packers-playoff-sunday-1007135 "Share on Twitter")

*   Copied!

![Image 3: RematchMain.jpg](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/f_auto/cardinals/ao2co6lrzw74l1ba1iv7.jpg)

The NFL announced the Cardinals will host the [Green Bay Packers](http://www.packers.com/) Sunday, Jan. 10,at University of Phoenix Stadium in the Wild Card round of the playoffs. Kickoff will be at 2:30 p.m. Arizona time and the game will air on FOX.

Tickets for the game will go on sale Monday for those in Arizona and on Tuesday everywhere else.

**TICKET INFORMATION**: Starting Monday at 7 a.m.Arizona time Cardinals-Packers playoff tickets will be available exclusively on-line and only to Arizona residents. These tickets can be purchased at [www.ticketmaster.com](http://www.ticketmaster.com/) and are available to customers with Arizona billing addresses only.

On Tuesday at 7 a.m., any remaining tickets will be available nationwide through Ticketmaster on-line as well as by phone. At 8:30 a.m. Tuesday, fans can purchase tickets in person at the Cardinals Tempe Training Facility box office and at the University of Phoenix Stadium box office. At that time they will also be available in-person at participating Ticketmaster outlets (hours vary by location).

There will be a limit of 8 tickets on all transactions.

CARDINALS PLAYOFF TICKET

 PURCHASE OPPORTUNITIES

DATE TIME HOW AVAILABLE

Tuesday, 1/5 7 a.m. Available everywhere, Internet and phone

Tuesday, 1/5 8:30 a.m.In-person at Univ. of Phoenix Stadium and Tempe box offices

Also at participating Ticketmaster locations (hours vary)

An Emotional March To New Orleans As Cardinals Outlast Packers
==============================================================

Warner has one of NFL's best games ever in 51-45 Wild Card win
--------------------------------------------------------------

 Jan 10, 2010 at 06:53 PM

![Image 3: Author Image](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_thumb_squared/f_auto/cardinals/i9mqqmnmpdemmytbkevx.jpg)

[Darren Urban](https://www.azcardinals.com/author/darren-urban)

azcardinals.com

[](http://www.twitter.com/cardschatter)[](mailto:askdarren@cardinals.nfl.net)

![Image 4: Linebacker Karlos Dansby begins to celebrate as he scores the game-winning touchdown Sunday in the Cards' 51-45 overtime playoff victory over the Packers.](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/f_auto/cardinals/ibem48y0iyhjgk3pxep7.jpg)

 Photo by Arizona Cardinals 

 Linebacker Karlos Dansby begins to celebrate as he scores the game-winning touchdown Sunday in the Cards' 51-45 overtime playoff victory over the Packers. 

Linebacker Karlos Dansby begins to celebrate as he scores the game-winning touchdown Sunday in the Cards' 51-45 overtime playoff victory over the Packers.

Michael Adams was crying, Clark Haggans was telling people the Cardinals had "dodged a bullet" and a shoeless Gabe Watson simply wore a big grin.

"That might be the game of the century," Watson said after the big defensive tackle jogged off the University of Phoenix Stadium field, having given away his cleats following the Cardinals' emotional 51-45 overtime win over the Packers in Sunday's Wild Card playoff game.

Arguing Watson's point might be fruitless. The ending alone was worth an NFL Network replay, when oft-picked-on cornerback Michael Adams – suffering through a horrendous game – drilled Packers quarterback Aaron Rodgers to force a fumble, which popped into the hands of linebacker Karlos Dansby for a 17-yard game-winning touchdown.

The final TD made it the highest-scoring playoff game in NFL history, and sends the Cards to play the top-seeded Saints in New Orleans Saturday at 2:30 p.m. Arizona time.

It's a short week, but the Cards weren't worrying about that yet.

"I fought for 65 minutes," safety Antrel Rolle said, "and I don't think I could have fought 66."

The teams totaled more than 1,000 yards of offense. Rodgers threw an interception on his first pass before finishing with 422 yards passing and four touchdowns – impressive numbers, yet eclipsed by Cardinals quarterback Kurt Warner's insane effort of 29-for-33 for 379 yards and five touchdowns without a turnover.

The teams combined for nine touchdowns in the second half and the brief overtime.

"The game was a blur in the second-half," safety Adrian Wilson said, shaking his head in amazement with slight grin on his face. "That was video-game-like."

The Cards had promised their Week 17 blowout loss to the same Packers wasn't important, and that was proven. Green Bay came into the game after finishing the season as a plus-24 in turnover ratio, yet the Cardinals forced two Packer turnovers in the first five minutes of the game.

With Warner playing as well as he did last postseason – and even without the injured Anquan Boldin, who sat out with knee and ankle injuries – the Arizona offense was scary good. At one point, the Cardinals held a 31-10 lead. Rookie Beanie Wells rushed for 92 yards as the Cards sliced up the NFL's No. 1 rushing defense for 156 yards on the ground.

In Boldin's sted, Steve Breaston (seven catches for 125 yards and a touchdown) and Early Doucet (6-77-2) stepped up, while wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald (6-82-2) overcame an early fumble.

"It was one of those games where I just felt great," Warner said. "I felt like I was seeing everything well and it accumulates into 51 points."

But the Packers, after their nervous foray into the postseason with many young players, started to score at will.

Green Bay sliced the lead to seven after using a successful onside kick to post back-to-back touchdowns, and when the Cards were forced into their only punt of the game early in the fourth quarter, Rodgers eventually made not one but two tying touchdown drives easy work.

"This is a hard game to swallow," Packers coach Mike McCarthy said. "It's a tough loss, but it sure was a great game to watch."

The final touchdown came with 1:52 left, in a game where that much time meant an eternity to get into field-goal range. Warner did exactly that, setting up Neil Rackers for a game-winning 34-yard try with 14 seconds left.

Except Rackers pulled it wide left.

"I haven't hit a ball left in two years," Rackers said. "I just snap-hooked it. Luckily my teammates came through in the clutch."

It didn't seem like it would be that simple. The Packers took a knee after the miss and the game seemingly was riding on the overtime coin flip, given the ease in which the offenses were moving. And then the Packers won the flip to take the ball.

"My reaction was like, 'Damn,' " Dansby said. "Everything was bouncing their way."

The feeling got worse when Rodgers, on first down, scrambled out of trouble and saw Greg Jennings wide open behind Rolle deep down the field. Rodgers' pass was barely overthrown.

"He threw it deep the one time, and I was like, 'Uh-oh,' " defensive lineman Darnell Dockett said. "But then coach made the right call at the right time, and we made a play."

The final play came on third-and-6 from Green Bay's 24-yard line, with the crowd – still deafening despite a smattering of green-and-gold – screaming for the defense. Adams, who left the field in tears after his emotional roller coaster of a day, came on the blitz and got to Rodgers before he could get rid of the ball.

Moments later, Dansby was in the end zone and the Cardinals were on their way to New Orleans.

"That's two really good playoff games that we have been in within the last two," coach Ken Whisenhunt said. "It is damn nice to win one of them instead of what happened in the Super Bowl."

All-points bulletin: Cardinals outscore Packers, 51-45
======================================================

By Sam Farmer 

Jan. 11, 2010 12 AM PT 

*

Reporting from Glendale, Ariz.—Kurt Warner was sharp as a cactus needle, but it was Arizona’s defense that punctured Green Bay’s Super Bowl dreams.

In an overtime game that put the wild in wild card -- a Sunday shootout featuring 13 touchdowns and a playoff-record 96 points -- the Cardinals won, 51-45, on linebacker Karlos Dansby’s 17-yard fumble return in sudden death.

The Cardinals launched their latest bid for the Lombardi Trophy with one of the most dramatic victories in franchise history.

“That’s two really good playoff games we’ve been in within a year,” said Arizona Coach Ken Whisenhunt, whose team lost the Super Bowl to Pittsburgh last February in the final minute. “It’s damn nice to win one of them.”

The Cardinals will play a divisional game Saturday at top-seeded New Orleans.

The Packers, who fought back to force overtime after trailing by three touchdowns in the third quarter, saw their season end against a backdrop of red jerseys and swirling white towels.

“It’s a tough loss,” said Green Bay Coach Mike McCarthy, whose team had pounded the Cardinals in an exhibition game and in a Week 17 finale. “It’s personally one of the toughest losses I’ve been a part of. . . . It’s a tough loss, but it sure was a great game to watch.”

It was, in fact, the only truly competitive playoff game of the weekend. The margin of victory in the weekend’s other three games averaged 16.3 points.

Although the Packers-Cardinals game was decided by a huge defensive play -- Michael Adams sacked Green Bay’s Aaron Rodgers on a corner blitz, stripping loose the ball -- it will be remembered for offensive pyrotechnics.

Arizona’s Kurt Warner further bolstered his case for the Hall of Fame by completing 29 of 33 passes for 379 yards and five touchdowns, recording a near-perfect passer rating of 154.1. He had more scoring passes than incompletions -- and that was without injured receiver Anquan Boldin.

“What more is there to say about Kurt?” Whisenhunt said. “He’s one of the best playoff quarterbacks of all time. We thought going into today that would be an advantage for us.”

It certainly didn’t hurt. Warner spread the ball among his receivers, helping each compile a personal highlight reel. Larry Fitzgerald and Early Doucet caught two touchdown passes each, and Steve Breaston caught one.

Said Warner: “Coming in as banged up as we were today, worried about how much they were going to play, how effective they were going to be, so many people across the board stepped up and made plays. That’s what it takes this time of year, and that’s what it takes to make runs.”

Warner’s performance eclipsed that of Rodgers, who was terrific in his own right, completing 28 of 42 for 422 yards and four touchdowns with an interception, and a 121.3 rating.

The scoring drives were so relentlessly efficient, especially down the stretch, that it seemed the last team to have the ball would win. So when Green Bay won the overtime coin toss and elected to receive, Whisenhunt felt a pang of dread.

“It was almost like, we will flip the coin and whoever wins the toss wins the game,” he said. “You don’t have to go out there and play it. I’m glad we did.”

But he said he had faith his players on the other side of the ball would come through, even though they had yielded nearly 500 yards of offense to the Packers.

“When we lost [the toss], I thought, ‘Our defense is going to make a play,’ ” he said. “I just believed . . . that maybe destiny was going to smile on us this time.”

It wouldn’t have come down to the defense had Arizona’s Neil Rackers made his 34-yard field-goal attempt with 14 seconds left in regulation. But he hooked that wide left, giving the Packers new life.

When the visitors got the ball to open the extra period, however, they couldn’t do a lot with it. Four plays into overtime, Rodgers was stripped and, as he was falling back, somehow kicked the ball up -- just where Dansby could latch on to it and rumble across the goal line.

“That gave me enough time to run up under it, get in the end zone, and seal the deal,” Dansby said.

The final play is sure to light up talk-radio switchboards all over Wisconsin and beyond, because TV replays showed Adams could have been flagged for grabbing Rodgers’ facemask.

Regardless, it’s over, and it was sweet redemption for Adams, who earlier missed a sack and twice was called for pass interference.

“I was just hoping he didn’t release the ball,” Adams said of Rodgers. “I mean, you can come 12 times, and 11 out of those 12 times he would get the ball out. That 12th chance, you get a chance to hit him, and I got my 12th chance.”

And it came at the 11th hour -- and none too soon for the Cardinals.
